name: Swedish Green
lede: Swedish green is an old trade name for Scheele's green, the copper arsenite pigment invented in Sweden in the 1770s, though one source links the name to a cobalt green instead.

sections.title: Two readings of one name
sections.body:
Swedish green is, in the Pigment Compendium's main entry, another name for [[scheele-s-green|Scheele's green]], a copper arsenite pigment [1][2]. The Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele (1742 to 1786) discovered it, and because it was first made in Sweden the color was tied to that country [1].

The sources do not fully agree. Fiedler and Bayard link Swedish green to Scheele's green, while Mayer connects it with the term [[cobalt-green|cobalt green]] [1]. The Pigment Compendium also lists Swedish green among names for cobalt-zinc compounds, so the name can point at two different materials [3]. We follow the compendium's main reading.

sections.title: How it was made
sections.body:
Scheele's results were published in 1778, but the exact method was kept secret so that he could profit [2]. The basic procedure mixed solutions of copper sulfate and arsenic oxide dissolved with potassium carbonate [2]. Later production in Germany used a slightly different process [2].

The compendium notes that the pigment gathered a great many names, possibly to hide its association with known toxicity, and lists mineral green and Swedish green among them [2]. That is a suggestion, not a documented fact. Scheele's green is poisonous because it holds arsenic, and later [[emerald-green|emerald green]] was often confused with it [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a mid yellow-green. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 10 hold it as a large enough patch, as photographed, and all fall in the 1800s and 1900s [4]. The first three are Matisse (1908), Gauguin (1886) and Pissarro (1898), the generation that took up bright greens [4]. A color match is not a pigment test [4]. We cannot tell from a photograph whether any of these painters used Scheele's green [4].

questions.q: Why is the pigment called Swedish green?
choices: It was first manufactured in Sweden by Scheele
It was dyed with Swedish birch bark
A king of Sweden chose it

choices: No, one source links it to cobalt green
